The studio had settled into a quiet rhythm. I began with a broad wash of ochre and umber along the lower third of the paper, letting the pigment settle into the paper’s grain. A fine brush returned to the background—the distant trees, the window frame, the soft curve of the lamp—and added subtle washes in pale blue and muted green. I watched the colors bleed together without becoming muddy, allowing the edges to retain a little more life.

Then came the sketch. With a pencil, I traced the shapes of the branches and leaves, keeping the lines loose and slightly uneven. Each mark was an honest observation of the studio: the way the light moved across the canvas, the faint dust motes caught in the air, the quiet rhythm of the room waking up. I did not try to make every detail perfect. Instead, I added small strokes of charcoal and graphite to the shadows where the brushwork had left little room. The darker areas became softer, the lighter regions gained depth.

By the end of the session, the paper looked like a sketchbook page: rough enough to feel alive, but finished enough to rest comfortably. ### The Forest’s First Whisper

Before the trees had learned their names, the forest was a long, thin line of breathing green. Moss crept over the roots like a slow river of silver, and the smallest bird had not yet learned to hide its song from the wind. Sunlight entered through the leaves as a slow, golden hand, carrying the warmth of a thousand nights together.

In this place, time did not move in straight lines but in circles. One autumn day, a branch would hold a leaf so long that it grew up from its own roots. In winter, the same branch would give it back. Each leaf was a promise, waiting for the rain to decide how it would begin again.

I walked among them, my boots quiet, and listened. There were no words here, only the slow exchange of breath between the earth, the trees, and the creatures who lived in their shadows. The wind moved through the branches like a traveler carrying a message from one forest to another.

Soon I would learn to listen more carefully. Some birds sing only when the world is quiet. The moss speaks in the color of the rain. And beneath the soil, something ancient is stirring, waiting for the first true beginning.

## The First Rain

I opened the notebook and wrote in the margin: the first rain.

That was the beginning of the collection. Not a grand statement, not a carefully chosen title, and certainly not a finished chapter. It was just a small beginning—the sound of water falling through the open window, the smell of damp earth beneath my feet, the way the light changed as the clouds opened.

I began with a simple goal: write one page of nature. But nature does not obey a clean script. It gathers in the corners of my thoughts, in the way the light moves across a window, in the pause between two birds, in the slow accumulation of a puddle. I wanted to capture that without making it perfect. I wanted to show the beginning rather than explain the whole.

So I wrote about the rain before I wrote about the trees. About the wind before the clouds. About the ordinary—dust, heat, shadows, the feeling of holding something that could not belong to me. I began with the sound:

A small bell struck.

It was the beginning of the collection, the first note I had recorded.

content:
The oak is still standing, stubborn as the old man who planted it. It remembers the winter when the branches bled red and smelled like wet earth. It remembers the café before the sign read “Open,” before the plastic chairs and neon light swallowed everything. It remembers the rain that came down in sheets and the way the ground shook beneath the sidewalk.

I wrote it down in my notebook, under the branch where the old oak was strongest. The tree has no face, but it has a history. The café has no name, but it has made people feel. Both belong to the neighborhood. Neither belongs to me unless I let them.

At seven sharp, I woke up. The house was quiet enough to hear the birds. I drank coffee while checking the poems from the natural-world collection. A bird had stopped at the window. Its yellow eyes were too bright for this room. I watched it for a long time. My hands shook. I kept writing. The poems were not beautiful in that way. They were honest. They were tired. They were mine.

At five, I ate dinner with Latoya. She talked about the community garden, how the old oak was getting another life, how the café was opening up, how we could make space for people instead of turning everything into performance. I listened. I did not say much.

At ten, I went home and went to bed. The night was cool enough that I felt warm. I dreamed of a tree, not a person. I dreamed of a café, not a place. I dreamed of a neighborhood, not a performance.

In the morning, I will check the oak again. I will write about it. I will not make it look perfect. I will leave room for the rain, the cracks, the birds, the people who walk past the sidewalk without knowing why. I will honor the old oak and the café without pretending they are my property. I will use them as a mirror, not as a trophy.

That is what I mean by “productive.” It does not mean writing the next masterpiece. It means writing enough so that tomorrow will not be empty. That means writing about the things that matter, even when they are not easy to explain. And that means listening to the neighbor beside me.

The oak tree in Café Display leaned toward the glass windows as if sharing the afternoon’s heat. Its branches stretched like dark fingers across the courtyard, each leaf a closed letter. Beneath it, the café sat in a small, silver room where the tables were made of polished wood and the light fell in long, patient strips. I had been here before, though I had never noticed the shape of the tree. I had always thought of the oak as a monument.

The poem collection had made me look at ordinary things with more care. The oak was ordinary enough, yet it held something extraordinary. Its bark was a map of old storms, every crack a memory that no one could read. The café below offered a simpler kind of shelter. A cup of coffee, the clink of silverware, the scent of roasted beans and rain on hot pavement. All of it was small, but it was not empty.

I had written a line once about the oak: “It stood against the city like a hand waiting to hold the world.” I had not been sure whether the hand was holding, or merely holding. The tree seemed to be giving.

Now I saw the oak not as a symbol, but as a neighbor. The café’s window was a small window into the world beyond, and the oak was a doorway into the world behind it. Their meeting created a space where the city could enter, and the world could enter the city.

I began to write the opening of my collection as if the tree were a character.

The oak stood at the edge of the town, a gray cathedral of roots and sunlight. Its branches reached for the sky, and the leaves whispered in a language the trees were not allowed to speak. At the café’s window, the oak looked down on the street, where the world was crowded with people, conversations, and the soft sounds of a place that had been built to keep everyone comfortable.

I had wanted to begin with the coffee. But a cup cannot tell the story of a tree. The oak had to speak first.

The oak’s roots were not merely underground; they were beneath the earth, beneath the pavement, beneath the houses, beneath the bus, beneath the rain, beneath the people who walked through the town. They reached for the dark, for the water, for the things that made life feel heavy enough to bear.

At the café, the table was set for two. The silverware caught the light, and the coffee was waiting, warm and strong, as if it had been holding a secret too long. I did not know what that secret was. I only knew that the oak had been there before, and that the tree had seen everything the people below had forgotten.

The wind moved through the leaves. It was not angry. It was carrying the scent of rain, the smell of earth waking up, the faint, metallic scent of something old and bright. It moved through the café, passed the table, and disappeared into the street.

I took a cup of coffee. The heat rose in my chest, and I felt small. I did not feel lonely. I felt like the oak, and the café, and the town, all of them were one room.

Outside, the oak opened one branch. It was not opening to invite the world in. It was opening because the room had grown too full to remain entirely closed.

I wrote the story of the oak as if the tree were a person, and I wrote the story of the café as if the coffee shop were a home. I wrote of the rain, of the coffee, of the light, of the silence, of the wind, of the people who came and went, of the oak’s roots, of the trees beyond, and of the space between them.

The story was not finished yet. It was still being written. The oak was still listening.

The studio was quiet, and I began with the smallest detail. The brush held a little more water than I’d planned, and as I swept across the paper, the paper lifted slightly. I lifted the paper and let it settle. The background became softer, and the edges softened too.

I stopped and looked at the page. The brush had done its job. The washes were not perfect, but they had softened the page and made the details feel more like part of the paper itself. I had changed the balance of the composition. The drawing had moved from being the main object to being the background.

I placed the paper back down and looked at it again. The finished piece had a quiet rhythm. I could hear the brush moving through the paper, and I could see the paper settling around it. The washes were not overpowering, and they had added depth without dominating the work.

## Paint and Sketch in the Studio

The studio was quiet enough to hear the pencil scrape against the board. I sharpened the fine brush, letting the steel tip cool and harden, then began with a light mark along the edge of the canvas. The first lines were tentative, almost invisible. I did not rush.

I painted first, sketching in the cool gray of morning light before I added color. Then I returned to the paper with a fine brush, sharpening the point with the edge of a pencil. The edges held themselves together when I defined them. I traced the rough outlines of my hand, the curve of my wrist, the small wrinkles in my skin. These were not photographs; they were memories made visible.

I sharpened the brush again, this time with deliberate pressure. The fine brush caught the paper in a sudden flash of black. One line. Then another. The paper felt alive beneath the marks.

By the time I finished, I was ready to begin again. I set down the pencil, wiped my hand on my apron, and returned to the canvas. There was no need for perfection. I only needed to begin.

As I refine the window frame, I introduce small touches of ochre and rose-gold watercolor. A few dry brush strokes catch the light on the glass, while a single fine line traces the edge of the chair beneath it.
